quiz.q: By default, where do the IP Allowlist/Blocklist policies read the caller's IP from?
quiz.explain: The IP expression is `#[attributes.headers['x-forwarded-for']]`. Postman sends this header automatically even if you don't add it.

quiz.q: A request comes from an IP that is not on the IP Allowlist. What response does the caller get?
quiz.explain: The IP policies reject with 403 and the message "The IP Address is invalid: <ip>".

quiz.q: You need to allow 100 developers whose IPs are in a range like 10.1.25.1–10.1.25.100. How do you configure the allowlist?
options: Use a CIDR range (with a slash), adding more rows for more ranges
Only one IP is allowed per policy
Put the range in the X-Forwarded-For header
quiz.explain: A range is given in CIDR notation, and there's no limit on rows — add more rows for more IPs or ranges.

quiz.q: Why can IP allowlisting be tricky for a consumer hosted in the cloud?
options: When a worker crashes and the app moves to a new worker, it gets a different IP
CIDR doesn't work in the cloud
quiz.explain: For availability another worker is started after a crash, and the new worker has a different IP, so it no longer matches the allowed list.

quiz.q: In JSON Threat Protection, what does the default value -1 mean?
options: No limit — applying all defaults is the same as not applying the policy
quiz.explain: Any negative number means no limit.

quiz.q: JSON Threat Protection has Maximum container depth = 1, and the request body is an object containing an array. What happens?
options: It is rejected with 400 — container depth exceeded, because object + array is depth 2
quiz.explain: First level object, second level array = depth 2. The class saw 400 "Container depth has been exceeded. Maximum allowed is: 1".

quiz.q: A student asks why JSON Threat Protection is needed when the APIkit Router validates the body. What's the answer?
options: APIkit validates only after the request is inside the app, when memory is already allocated; the policy rejects it at the gateway
The policy is faster because it skips the Listener's port
They do exactly the same thing
quiz.explain: Between the Listener and the APIkit Router, memory is already used for attributes and payload; the policy stops the request before it reaches the app.

quiz.q: Rate Limiting is set to 3 requests per 1 minute. What does the 4th request in that minute get?
options: 429 Too Many Requests — "Quota has been exceeded"
quiz.explain: Requests over the limit are rejected straight away with 429; after the minute passes it works again.

quiz.q: You try to add Rate Limiting SLA to an API that already has a separate Client ID Enforcement policy. What happens?
options: A conflict is highlighted — Rate Limiting SLA already includes client ID enforcement
Client ID Enforcement is converted to SLA automatically
Rate Limiting SLA ignores client IDs
quiz.explain: Rate Limiting SLA is client ID enforcement + rate limiting combined, so it can't coexist with a separate Client ID Enforcement policy.

quiz.q: An existing consumer must be moved to the gold SLA tier. How was this done in class?
options: Edit the tier field on the existing contract
Revoke and delete the old contract, then request access again in Exchange choosing the tier
Redeploy the app with a new property
quiz.explain: A tier is chosen when requesting access, so an existing consumer needs a new contract. Manual-approval tiers must then be approved in Contracts.

quiz.q: In Spike Control, when is a queued request finally rejected?
options: When the queue is full or the delay attempts are exhausted with no quota available
Never — it is always processed eventually
quiz.explain: Spike Control (throttling) queues extra requests and retries after the delay time; it rejects only when the queuing limit is reached or attempts run out.

quiz.q: Which policy order did the class describe as logical?
options: Basic auth → JSON threat protection → rate limiting
Rate limiting → JSON threat protection → basic auth
JSON threat protection → basic auth → rate limiting
quiz.explain: Policies run in the listed order (reorder with the arrows); rate limiting, then threat protection, then authentication.

cards.back: Allowlist lets only listed IPs/ranges through; blocklist rejects the listed ones. Both read `X-Forwarded-For` by default and reject with **403**.

cards.front: Why is IP allowlisting tricky for cloud consumers?
cards.back: Cloud workers get new IPs when replaced (e.g. after a crash), so a consumer's IP can change and stop matching.

cards.front: Delay time / delay attempts / queuing limit
cards.back: Delay: wait between retries (keep small, ~1 s). Attempts: retries before rejecting (2–3). Queuing limit: how many requests may wait.
Rate limiting rejects extra requests immediately (429). Spike control queues and retries; rejects only when the queue is full or attempts run out.
